summary:
New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while the territory legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are therefore French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.

Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.

Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.

Placement of detainees follows the legal gender marker rather than anatomy: Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice places trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees (BuzzFeed News, 12 January 2018). The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.

France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, reported on 25 May 2021 a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.
tangentialFactors:
The formal position and the lived position diverge for detainees. Anti-discrimination protection and marriage equality are settled points of French law, while the same legal system that supplies them has been found by its own oversight body to permit serious violations of transgender detainees' rights.

The named prisons in the CGLPL material are mainland French establishments, and the BuzzFeed reporting concerns French prisons generally. Neither source describes conditions inside New Caledonia's own detention facilities, so the mainland findings indicate the standard of the applicable framework rather than conditions on the ground here.

Because the operative provisions are French statutes, any change enacted in Paris would alter the position in New Caledonia without local legislative action; the territory's own legislature does not control these rules.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Caledonia are subject to the French Penal Code's discrimination provisions, including the gender-identity ground added in 2012 and reworded in 2016, and to the French criminal procedure rules governing the placement of detainees.

Civil-status matters, including marriage and the documents that record it, fall under French law, so residents marry under the 2013 statute and obtain civil-status records through the French system.

The CGLPL's mandate covers French places of deprivation of liberty, which includes establishments in the collectivity; its inspection and referral machinery is available to residents held here as well as on the mainland.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records an instance of the gender-identity discrimination provision being invoked in New Caledonia, and no enforcement or prosecution data for the territory is available here.

Whether any detainee in New Caledonia has been placed according to the Article D248 rule, and how local facilities house trans detainees, is unresolved: the sources describe the French framework and mainland practice only.

There is no sourced information here on hate-crime sentencing enhancement as applied in the collectivity, on procedures for changing gender markers on identity documents, or on access to gender-affirming care for residents and visitors.
